text: The "be prepared to explain your work at any time" rule is what makes this whole policy work. A lot of AI policies in academia right now are either blanket bans that pretend the technology doesn't exist or open-door policies with no accountability. This one threads the needle perfectly — use AI all you want, but if you can't walk a TA through your reasoning, you didn't learn anything and it'll show. The 20% relative grading component is also quietly brilliant because it creates a natural incentive to iterate rather than just accept the first output. When everyone has access to the same tools, the differentiator becomes how thoughtfully you use them — which is exactly the mindset a prompt engineering course should be building. This policy honestly deserves to be a template for other professors figuring out how to handle AI in their classrooms. It treats students like professionals who will be using these tools in their careers, not like cheaters who need to be policed.

text:
This is honestly one of the most refreshing AI policies I've heard from an educator. Instead of banning it or ignoring it, he's treating it like the real-world tool it actually is. Your boss doesn't care if AI helped you; they care if the work is good. The part about explaining what you turned in is a built-in filter that separates people who used AI as a shortcut from people who actually learned something from it.
The relative grading component is what's really going to humble people, though. A lot of students assume that using AI automatically means great work, but when everyone has access to the same tools, the baseline shifts upward for the whole class. You're no longer just competing against a rubric, you're competing against every other student who also had AI. That's a completely different kind of pressure, and honestly, a much more accurate preview of the real world.
